Hosios Loukas is a walled monastery near the town of Distomo in Boeotia, central Greece, founded in the mid 10th century around the tomb of a local hermit, Saint Luke of Steiris, who died in 953. Its main church, built in the early 11th century, is one of the finest surviving buildings of Middle Byzantine art.

The monastery has two churches joined together. The larger, the katholikon, is a domed church whose upper walls and vaults are covered with mosaics on a gold ground: Christ, the Virgin, saints and gospel scenes, with coloured marble below. Its plan, with the dome resting on corner arches over a square hall, was copied in later churches in Greece.

With Daphni near Athens and Nea Moni on Chios, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1990. The three are the best places to see the art of the Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian emperors, since most churches of that time in Constantinople were lost or changed.
